notes.meaning: David leads God's people in praise at Zion, the hill where God's house stood. The word for "awaits" can also mean "is silent." Praise stands ready like a servant, or falls quiet because no words are big enough for God's goodness. The people also promise to keep the vows they made to God when they asked for His help.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some commentators doubt that David wrote this psalm. They point out that it speaks of the Temple and its courts, which were built after his time.

notes.meaning: Hearing prayer is part of who God is. It is one of His titles of honor. Because He listens, people of every nation will come to Him. Many have read this as a promise that non-Jewish peoples (the Gentiles) would one day come to God through Christ.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Ellicott accepts that the verse points to the gospel spreading to all nations. But he thinks the psalmist himself meant something narrower: every nation may pray to God, while praise in Zion was Israel's special privilege.

notes.meaning: Sins can pile up until they feel too strong for us. We cannot balance them with any goodness of our own. Yet God atones for them, which means He covers them and makes things right. His free mercy does this, and He provides the way Himself. Christian writers see this pointing ahead to Christ's sacrifice.

The person God chooses and brings close to Himself is truly happy. That person may live near Him, the way priests lived and served in His house. Such a person comes near by God's free choice, not by their own merit. Then the psalm changes from "he" to "we." All God's people share in the rich goodness of His house.

differ.view: God freely chooses certain people. By His special grace He draws them near and makes them able to come.
Believers are chosen for Christ's sake and accepted in Him, not because of anything in themselves.
The chosen ones here are the priests picked to serve at God's house. Ordinary worshippers still share in its blessings.
The one chosen is Israel as a people, brought back into the blessings of God's covenant (His binding promise).

notes.meaning: God answers His people's prayers with awesome acts. Often these are acts of judgment against their enemies, and He always does what is right. He is the God who saves them. People everywhere can trust Him, even in the farthest lands and out on the sea.
God set the mountains firmly in place by His own strength. He keeps them standing, as if He had wrapped a belt of power around them. Believers can rest in that same strength.
God quiets the roaring sea and its crashing waves. Jesus showed this same power when He calmed the storm. In the same way, God calms nations in uproar and holds back people who would cause chaos.

Even people in faraway lands feel awe at God's signs, such as storms and the steady rule of day and night. These signs show there is a God above all. Both morning and evening are His gifts. Morning brings light for work, and evening brings rest. So He makes sunrise and sunset sing for joy.

God visits the earth like a caring gardener and waters it. "The streams of God" means the rain. God sends it from a supply that never runs dry. This is how He prepares the grain that feeds His people.

Rain soaks the plowed ground. It breaks down the hard clumps and softens the soil so seed can sprout. God then blesses the young plants as they grow. Some writers also see here a picture of the Holy Spirit softening hard hearts.
A full harvest is like a crown on the year. It comes from God's goodness, which we have not earned. Wherever God passes, He leaves plenty behind, as if His very footsteps dripped with richness.
God's rain falls even on wild land where no one farms. It gives grass for the animals there. Everywhere the hills look green and glad, as if they were dressed for a party.

The fields are so full of sheep that they look covered with them. The valleys are filled with grain. All creation seems to shout and sing God's praise for His kindness. There was no joy like the joy of harvest.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Keil and Delitzsch argue that fields cannot sing. They think the ones shouting and singing are the people, who rejoice over the harvest.
